This is a short story, but it underscores the importance of how good weight control will save your life.

I live in a very isolated location. We're talking Sub-Arctic. So, I got to go hunting with an older, more experienced fella who we will call "dude", to improve my hunting and outdoor skills. Dude is former Ranger and taught outdoor skills to various military and police over the years but is getting up there in years and is starting to finally slow down a bit. We decided to head up some the exploration roads heading into the mountains, meaning we are mounted on ATV's. Both of us know that gear can make or break a trip, however, weight of gear is critical as you may have to hump it all out if the machine breaks down.

Day before heading out Dude phones me and tells me that his school chum "Ham" is gonna tag along. That's cool, I'm in for some of that low fat moosie reward at all cost. Day of, I'm out to the bush and meet Dude at the prearranged location. Ham shows up one whole hour late, gets out of his truck and breathlessly waddling to the back of his truck. Ham literally can't walk. Realizing this could go really poorly, I lean over to Dude and ask if Ham is gonna be ok with this trip. He whispers back that Ham has two replacement hips, a buggered knee, and Type 2. But, since we are mechanized Ham should be fine. Alright, cool. We help Ham onto his machine, which is loaded to the gills with gear. As the trip and day progress, we find that his gear is full of sweet, sugary goodness and he never stops shoveling it into his maw. Jeezus, that can't be good for the type 2.

The day passes uneventfully, but, sadly no moose for us. Coming back along a mountain ridge, Dude and I decide to pull off and run up to the summit to get a GPS fix. Ham has been following us really well the whole trip and has been a non-issue. However, in the twilight, he totally misses our machines pulled off to the side of the trail and keeps racing down the mountain. Dude and I run down from the summit, start our ATV's, and follow Ham down. Staying together is paramount to staying safe.

Part way down, heading into a switchback, Dude is about 6 seconds ahead. He suddenly swerves around something in the middle of the road and slides to a stop. Holy crap it's Ham's ATV! Once I stop, I realize that Ham's pinned unconscious under the damn thing. It's still running, fuel and oil are pouring out all over Ham. Dude is far to old to be doing this crap but he's literally holding the ATV from rolling down on Ham. "fucking grab him!" Dude screams as I grab Ham and drag him out from underneath. Ham is over 300lbs. I can feel my back popping as I drag him down hill. Ran back to the machine and helped Dude roll it back over and shut it down. Transportation is critical since we are 30km, a river crossing, and another mountain range from the highway. Dude and I are now hurting pretty bad as I start in on first aid and Dude gets the sat comm going. Gonna put the shitty red cross first aid to work... first step is to see if he's awake. Nope. I check for pulse, can't find any at the neck or wrist, too much fat. Check his eyes, got response there and he's "breathing". Well, time for a body check. and Ham has got so much fat that I can't tell if anything is broken. It's like pushing on a marshmallow. I have no choice but to assume his back is broken. About this time he comes to but seems really confused. I quick memory check, but everything seems ok-enough. A helicopter is going to be around $10,000 and a cold night in the bush at 6000ft. Fuck that. As we talk with Ham it becomes apparent that he hit a rock and flipped his machine, so at least we know that it wasn't health related. A quick mobility check and he actually passes so we decide to ride out. We successfully made it out before the early morning hours and I drove him to the nearest hospital 3hrs away.

Though turning out well enough, the trip was totally pooched. In my opinion, Ham risked his life and our health/injury in a couple of ways: 1. He was too heavy and immobile for the technical riding that we were doing. His weight unbalanced the center of gravity of the machine, and systemic injury caused by his weight reduced his capacity to move effectively when the machine became unbalanced. 2. His weight and poor health made our efforts to prevent further injury and render effective first aid nearly impossible simply by being too heavy and resistant to the determination life signs.

I'm sorry that my writing sucks, but I have more stories with this guy too.
